content: 1. Mary Care in Addis Ababa published a study in 2004 in the journal Sexually Transmitted Infections, volume 80, issue 5, pages 392-394. 2. Cheluget B, Joesoef MR, Marum LH, Wandera C, Ryan CA, De Cock KM, and colleagues conducted research on the changing patterns of sexually transmitted disease syndromes in Kenya following the introduction of a syndromic management program. This study was published in Sexually Transmitted Diseases in 2004, volume 31, issue 9, pages 522-525. 3. Chilongozi DA, Daly CC, Franco L, Liomba NG, and Dallabetta G performed a survey on the case management of sexually transmitted diseases in Malawi. Their findings were published in the International Journal of STD & AIDS in 1996, volume 7, issue 4, pages 269-275. 4. Behets FM, Liomba G, Lule G, Dallabetta G, Hoffman IF, Hamilton HA, and colleagues conducted a field study on genital ulcer disease and its implications for sexually transmitted diseases and HIV control in Malawi. This study appeared in the Journal of Infectious Diseases in 1995, volume 171, issue 2, pages 451-455. 5. Garcia PJ, Gotuzzo E, Hughes JP, and Holmes KK evaluated the syndromic management of sexually transmitted diseases in pharmacies through a randomized intervention trial. Their work was published in Sexually Transmitted Infections in 1998, volume 74, Supplement 1, pages S153-S158. 6. Goel SS studied the syndromic management approach for sexually transmitted diseases in rural populations. The findings were published in the Indian Journal of Sexually Transmitted Diseases in 2012, volume 33, issue 2, pages 146-147. 7. Mertens TE, Smith GD, Kantharaj K, Mugrditchian D, and Radhakrishnan KM observed consultations for sexually transmitted diseases in India. Their research was published in Public Health in 1998, volume 112, issue 2, pages 123-128. 8. Sharma K, Chavan Y, Aras R, and Khismatrao D examined the syndromic management of sexually transmitted diseases in a male health clinic within a primary healthcare setting. Their study was published in the Indian Journal of Sexually Transmitted Diseases in 2011, volume 32, issue 2, pages 136-137. 9. Tankhiwale SS and Chavan SP conducted a comparative study of syndromic and etiological diagnoses of sexually transmitted infections, excluding HIV, among attendees of a sexually transmitted infection and reproductive tract infection clinic in central India. Their findings were published in the International Journal of Medicine and Public Health in 2013, volume 3, issue 4, pages 347-351. 10. Iipinge SN and Pretorius L assessed the delivery and quality of sexually transmitted infection treatment by private general practitioners in Windhoek, Namibia. Their study was published in the Global Journal of Health Science in 2012, volume 4, issue 5, pages 156-171. 11. Lule G, Behets FMT, Hoffman IF, Liomba G, Dallabetta G, Hamilton HA, and colleagues evaluated effective and affordable antibiotic regimens for sexually transmitted disease patients in Malawi. Their findings were published in the Malawi Medical Journal in 1998, volume 11, pages 50-55. 12. Machiha A, Mugurungi O, Tshimanga M, Kilmarx P, Mungati M, Nyakura J, and colleagues investigated the etiology of genital ulcer disease and its association with HIV infection in Zimbabwe. Their study was published in Sexually Transmitted Infections in 2015, volume 91, page A157. 13. Mahmood MA and Saniotis A explored the use of syndromic management algorithms for sexually transmitted infections and reproductive tract infections in community settings in Karachi. Their research was published in the Journal of the Pakistan Medical Association in 2011, volume 61, issue 5, pages 453-457. 14. Mark J, Hariri S, Ilunga R, Forhan S, Likibi M, MLK, and colleagues evaluated sexually transmitted infection clinical services in Gauteng Province, South Africa, focusing on the knowledge, attitudes, and beliefs of healthcare providers. Their findings were published in Sexually Transmitted Infections in 2011, volume 87, pages A92-A93. 15. Mathews C, van Rensburg A, and Coetzee N assessed the sensitivity of a syndromic management approach in detecting sexually transmitted diseases in patients at a public health clinic in Cape Town. Their study was published in the South African Medical Journal in 1998, volume 88, issue 10, pages 1337-1340. 16. Moodley P, Sturm PD, Vanmali T, Wilkinson D, Connolly C, and Sturm AW examined the association between HIV-1 infection, the etiology of genital ulcer disease, and response to syndromic management. Their research was published in Sexually Transmitted Diseases in 2003, volume 30, issue 3, pages 241-245. 17. Schneider H, Blaauw D, Dartnall E, Coetzee DJ, and Ballard RC analyzed sexually transmitted disease care in the South African private health sector. Their findings were published in the South African Medical Journal in 2001, volume 91, issue 2, pages 151-156. 18. Moherdaui F, Vuylsteke B, Siqueira LF, dos Santos Junior MQ, Jardim ML, de Brito AM, and colleagues validated national algorithms for diagnosing sexually transmitted diseases in Brazil through a multicenter study. Their research was published in Sexually Transmitted Infections in 1998, volume 74, Supplement 1, pages S38-S43. 19. Steen R, Soliman C, Mujyambwani A, Twagirakristu JB, Bucyana S, Grundmann C, and colleagues shared practical insights on upgrading sexually transmitted disease services based on experiences from primary healthcare facilities in two Rwandan towns. Their findings were published in Sexually Transmitted Infections in 1998, volume 74, Supplement 1, pages S159-S165. 20. Meheus A, Van Dyck E, Ursi JP, Ballard RC, and Piot P investigated the etiology of genital ulcerations in Swaziland. Their study was published in Sexually Transmitted Diseases in 1983, volume 10, issue 1, pages 33-35.
